0.title: Wealth, Generosity, and the Kingdom of God
0.essay:
Jesus said a great deal about money. Not because he was preoccupied with finance, but because he understood the heart, and money is one of the most reliable windows into it.

Where your treasure is

“For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21). Show me what you spend your money on, and you have shown me what you love.

Not money, but the love of it

The church has always struggled with money. Not because money is evil. It is not: God “richly provides us with everything to enjoy” (1 Timothy 6:17). The problem is disordered desire. “For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils” (1 Timothy 6:10). And in a consumer culture that defines life by acquisition and comfort, that disorder is both universal and invisible. We absorb its assumptions without noticing, and our relationship with money often looks more like the world than the kingdom.

What this study is

This is not a financial planning course. It is a look at what the Bible says about wealth, contentment, generosity, justice and stewardship. We will consider money as a gift to receive with gratitude, a test to face with integrity, a tool to use for the kingdom, and a danger to resist with vigilance.

The goal is not guilt but freedom: the freedom of someone who has heard Jesus say, “You cannot serve God and money” (Matthew 6:24), and has chosen to serve God.

Along the way we will draw on Tim Keller’s Generous Justice, Randy Alcorn’s The Treasure Principle, Craig Blomberg’s Neither Poverty nor Riches, and the wider Reformed tradition on vocation and stewardship.

The chapters

Money as Gift: created goodness and the danger of idolatry. Contentment: the lost art of enough. Generosity: the grace of giving. Justice and the Poor: money as a kingdom tool. Debt, Work, and Integrity: practical wisdom. And Eternal Perspective: laying up treasure in heaven.

For reflection

If someone read your bank statement for the last three months, what would they conclude you love?

1.title: Money as Gift: Created Goodness and the Danger of Idolatry
1.essay:
The first thing Scripture says about the material world is that it is good. The second, after the fall, is that we are prone to worship it.

Created good

God created the physical world, including the potential for wealth, and declared it “very good” (Genesis 1:31). That rules out treating wealth as inherently corrupt or the material world as a prison to escape. Creation is good. Work is good. Trade is good. The ability to earn, save, invest and give is a gift from the Creator to his image-bearers.

When money has us

Yet the fall has deeply distorted our relationship with material things. What was meant to be received as a gift from a good Father has become a source of security, identity and ultimate meaning. We look to wealth for what only God can give: safety, significance and sufficiency. That is idolatry. Not because we have money, but because money has us. The idol is not the coins themselves, but the trust we place in them and the comfort we demand from them.

Tim Keller observes that everyone has something that functions as their “righteousness,” the thing that makes them feel worthy. For many in the modern West, that thing is financial security. When it is threatened, we panic. When it is achieved, we feel we can finally breathe.

Hope in the right place

Paul writes, “As for the rich in this present age, charge them not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy” (1 Timothy 6:17). He does not tell the rich to give everything away. He tells them where to put their hope.

Wealth is uncertain. Markets crash, illness strikes, inflation bites, and death comes to all. To rest your hope on something uncertain is to live perpetually anxious. God is the source; wealth is only a channel. When the channel is treated as the source, idolatry has arrived. When the source is trusted, the channel can be enjoyed and given away freely.

Great gain

Paul’s definition of gain is deliberately subversive: “But godliness with contentment is great gain, for we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world. But if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content” (1 Timothy 6:6–8). We arrived with nothing and will leave with nothing, so the game of acquisition is played with borrowed chips.

Contentment is not the absence of desire. It is the presence of enough, and “enough” is defined not by the market but by the God who promises, “my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:19).

Who gave you the power?

Moses warned Israel about the temptation of prosperous seasons: the story that says, “I worked hard, I was clever, I succeeded.” Deuteronomy shatters it: “You shall remember the LORD your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth” (Deuteronomy 8:18). The capacity to work, the intelligence to succeed, the health to keep going and the opportunities that opened were all gifts. That does not make effort irrelevant. But it makes pride impossible, and gratitude the only fitting response.

Think of a successful entrepreneur in a Bible study who hears, for the first time, that God gave him both his talent and his opportunities. Something shifts. He stops thinking of his company as his achievement and starts thinking of it as his stewardship. His decisions about giving, about how he treats his staff, and about how he does business begin to look different. A gift received with gratitude is always used more wisely than an achievement clutched as a possession.

Doctrines that free us

The doctrine of creation tells us money is a gift. The doctrine of providence tells us it is held in God’s hands. The doctrine of sin explains why we worship it. And the doctrine of redemption sets us free from it. The Heidelberg Catechism teaches that God upholds and governs heaven and earth and all creatures by his fatherly hand, so that riches and poverty come to us not by chance but from him. That is humbling, because we did not earn it alone. And it is liberating, because we do not need to clutch it.

The richest gift

The gospel does not confront money’s grip with poverty, but with a different kind of wealth. “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9).

Jesus, eternally rich in the glory of God, became poor: born in borrowed space, a refugee in Egypt, dependent on others’ hospitality, dying stripped on a cross. He did this so that we might receive the imperishable riches of reconciliation with God, adoption as his children and an eternal inheritance. When we really grasp this, money’s grip on our hearts loosens. We cannot be gripped by the wealth of Christ and the wealth of the world at the same time.

For reflection

What do you look to money for: safety, significance, sufficiency? How would remembering that God gives you the power to get wealth change the way you hold what you have?

2.title: Contentment: The Lost Art of Enough
2.essay:
Paul wrote, “I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content” (Philippians 4:11). He wrote it from prison.

A learned secret

This is not the contentment of a man who has everything. It is the contentment of a man who has found that Christ is enough regardless of everything. And notice the words: I have learned. It was not natural or automatic. Contentment is a discipline, a skill formed by practice and grace.

Paul had known both comfort and deprivation: the status of a respected Pharisee, and the beatings, shipwrecks, prisons and hunger of an apostle. He goes on, “I have learned the secret of facing plenty and hunger, abundance and need” (Philippians 4:12). Contentment is not a function of circumstance but of relationship with Christ.

Then comes the verse so often quoted out of context: “I can do all things through him who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:13). In context, it is not about athletic achievement. It is about the strength to be content in poverty and the wisdom to hold abundance loosely.

Not Stoic indifference

In the ancient world, as in ours, contentment was countercultural. The Stoics sought it through indifference to circumstances. Paul found it through Christ’s strength flowing into him. Christian contentment does not turn away from the material world, as if things were evil. It receives what we have as a gift and finds its deepest satisfaction in Christ rather than in things.

A radical act

In a consumer culture, contentment is a radical act. The whole machinery of advertising is designed to make us discontent: to make us feel that life is incomplete without the next purchase, upgrade or experience. Contentment resists that machinery.

Be on your guard

Jesus warned, “Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions” (Luke 12:15). Covetousness is not a spectacular sin. It is a creeping one. It rarely announces itself. It wears the clothes of reasonable desires, legitimate ambitions and understandable comparisons. That is why Jesus says, be on your guard.

And then he gives the foundation of contentment: life does not consist in possessions. Not enhanced by them, not completed by them, not secured by them. To believe that is to be free.

He followed this with a story about a rich farmer whose crops did so well that he planned bigger barns and a life of ease. God said to him, “Fool! This night your soul is required of you” (Luke 12:20). The man had planned everything except the one thing that mattered.

The root and the snare

Paul writes, “But those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare, into many senseless and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils” (1 Timothy 6:9–10). The verse is often misquoted. It is not money, but the love of money, that is the root. Paul traces the problem to desire, before a single coin is gained. The craving itself is the snare. “It is through this craving that some have wandered away from the faith” (1 Timothy 6:10).

The antidote is not asceticism, but contentment: replacing the love of money with love for God, and the craving for wealth with enjoyment of his gifts.

He will never leave you

Hebrews gives the deepest ground of contentment: “Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have” (Hebrews 13:5). Why? Because God “has said, ‘I will never leave you nor forsake you.’” That promise echoes what God told Israel and Joshua as they faced an uncertain future (Deuteronomy 31:6; Joshua 1:5).

If God is always present, then the worst that can happen — financial ruin, poverty, loss — cannot take away the best thing: God himself. Contentment is not indifference. It is faith in the abiding presence of the One who is better than anything money can buy.

Discontent as unbelief

The Westminster Larger Catechism lists “discontentment with our own estate” and “envying and grieving at the good of our neighbour” among the sins against the tenth commandment. Discontent is a sin because it is a failure of faith. It says, in effect, “What God has given me is not enough, and he is not enough.” Only a deep conviction of God’s providence overcomes the fear of poverty, and that conviction frees us to give away what we have been given.

Enough is as good as a feast

Randy Alcorn puts it simply: you can’t take it with you, but you can send it on ahead. A person with an eternal perspective is free to give, free to simplify, free to discover that life does not consist in possessions.

Think of a family who decide to live on eighty per cent of their income and give away twenty, not as a rule but as a regular practice of gratitude. After five years they discover something surprising. They feel richer, not poorer. Giving has broken the power of accumulation over them, and they have learned to enjoy simpler pleasures. Their children grow up with a different relationship to money from their friends: not anxious, not acquisitive, but generous. As the old proverb says, enough is as good as a feast.

For reflection

Where is covetousness creeping into your life in the clothes of a “reasonable desire”? What would it look like to learn contentment in your present situation?

3.title: Generosity: The Grace of Giving
3.essay:
Generosity is not first a financial practice. It is a way of reflecting the character of a God who gives.

A giving God

God so loved the world that he gave his only Son (John 3:16). He gives wisdom “generously to all without reproach” (James 1:5). He richly provides us with everything to enjoy. The most generous act in history was the giving of the Son, and all Christian generosity is a response to that gift and a sharing in it.

The Macedonians

The New Testament’s longest treatment of giving is 2 Corinthians 8–9, where Paul encourages the Corinthians to complete their promised gift to the poor believers in Jerusalem. His argument is entirely theological. He does not manipulate or use guilt.

He tells the story of the Macedonian churches: “for in a severe test of affliction, their abundance of joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part” (2 Corinthians 8:2). Extreme poverty plus abundant joy produced overflowing generosity. They gave “beyond their means” (2 Corinthians 8:3). The economics make no sense, until Paul explains: “they gave themselves first to the Lord” (2 Corinthians 8:5).

The sequence is everything. Generosity that does not begin with surrender to God is philanthropy: admirable, but not transforming. Generosity that begins with “Lord, I am yours, and all I have is yours” produces giving that astonishes even an apostle.

Then Paul points to Jesus: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9). The model for giving is the gospel.

Sowing and reaping

“The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully. Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:6–7).

The harvest is in God’s hands, and it often surprises us in its form. It is not a promise of financial profit. Paul says God makes grace abound “so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work” (2 Corinthians 9:8), and “You will be enriched in every way to be generous in every way” (2 Corinthians 9:11). Givers are enriched so that they can be more generous, not more comfortable. And the goal is thanksgiving to God, overflowing from those who are helped.

The manner of giving matters as much as the amount. Not reluctantly. Not under pressure. Cheerfully. That is the sign of a heart that has understood the grace it has received.

The paradox of the open hand

“One gives freely, yet grows all the richer; another withholds what he should give, and only suffers want. Whoever brings blessing will be enriched, and one who waters will himself be watered” (Proverbs 11:24–25). This is not a prosperity-gospel promise. It is a wisdom observation about a paradox. The closed fist impoverishes and the open hand enriches, though not always in money. The generous person grows richer in relationships, peace, character and the joy of being used by God. The one who withholds suffers the poverty of a closed heart.

The widow’s coins

Jesus watched people giving at the temple. A poor widow put in two tiny copper coins. He said, “Truly, I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all of them. For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty put in all she had to live on” (Luke 21:3–4).

Jesus measures giving by proportion and sacrifice, not by size. That does not mean large gifts do not matter; the wealthy have greater capacity and greater responsibility. But God looks at the heart behind the gift. A good rule of thumb: give enough that it costs you something.

Tithing and beyond

Many Christians find the Old Testament tithe, a tenth, a helpful starting point. The New Testament does not lay down a fixed percentage, but it calls for giving that is regular, proportionate, sacrificial and cheerful. For many in wealthy nations, a tenth will be a floor, not a ceiling.

Gratitude, not guilt

The Reformed tradition grounds generosity in grace. Calvin taught that the proper response to God’s grace is gratitude, and that generosity is one of its clearest proofs. The Westminster Larger Catechism lists among the duties of the eighth commandment “giving and lending freely, according to our abilities, and the necessities of others.” Richard Baxter’s Christian Directory gave detailed guidance on giving in proportion to need and income. The New Testament standard can be summed up simply: give enough that it costs you, give joyfully, and let the gospel, not guilt, be the motive.

Whose money?

R. G. LeTourneau, the American engineer and businessman who eventually gave ninety per cent of his income to Christian work, used to say that the question was not how much of his money he gave to God, but how much of God’s money he kept for himself. He had grasped that the money was never his. It was entrusted to him. That reframing turns giving from sacrifice into stewardship.

Think of a pastor who preaches a series on generosity and, at the end, takes no pledges. He simply says, “Go home and pray. Ask God what he wants you to give. Then give that.” The following year, giving rises more than any campaign had ever achieved.

For reflection

Have you given yourself “first to the Lord”? Is your giving regular, proportionate, sacrificial and cheerful? What would it mean to ask God what he wants you to give, and then give that?

4.title: Justice and the Poor: Money as a Kingdom Tool
4.essay:
The Bible speaks about the poor again and again. A God who is perfectly just and perfectly merciful cannot be indifferent to their suffering, and neither can his people.

Built into the law

Care for the poor is not an optional extra in the Christian faith. It is part of the fabric of covenant faithfulness. In the law of Moses it is built in: gleaning rights for the poor at harvest (Leviticus 19:9–10), the year of Jubilee (Leviticus 25), the cancelling of debts every seventh year (Deuteronomy 15:1–11), and strict limits on exploiting workers and borrowers. “You shall not oppress a hired worker who is poor and needy” (Deuteronomy 24:14). “You shall give him his wages on the same day, before the sun sets” (Deuteronomy 24:15).

The prophets’ fire

The prophets thunder against economic injustice with an almost uncomfortable passion. “Woe to those who join house to house, who add field to field” (Isaiah 5:8), buying up land until the poor have nowhere left. Amos condemns Israel “because they sell the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals” (Amos 2:6).

Through Isaiah, God redefines religious devotion: “Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free” (Isaiah 58:6). “Is it not to share your bread with the hungry and bring the homeless poor into your house” (Isaiah 58:7). Religious performance divorced from justice is worthless. The worship God accepts flows out into generosity and solidarity with the poor.

Lending to the LORD

“Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed” (Proverbs 19:17). That is a startling verse. Giving to the poor is not charity looking down, but a loan to the Almighty, the most reliable debtor in the universe. Jesus said the same: “as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40).

The man at the gate

Jesus told of a rich man who feasted every day, “And at his gate was laid a poor man named Lazarus, covered with sores” (Luke 16:20). The rich man’s sin was not his wealth but his indifference. The poor man had a name, a story, the dignity of God’s image. The gate between them was small. The rich man passed it every day and never crossed it. After death the reversal was total: the one who had everything lost everything, and the one who had nothing was carried to Abraham’s side. The gospel is not against wealth. It is against the blindness wealth can produce.

Faith that works

James is relentlessly concrete. If a brother or sister is “poorly clothed and lacking in daily food,” and you wish them well “without giving them the things needed for the body, what good is that?” (James 2:15–16). His verdict: “So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead” (James 2:17).

James is not teaching that works save. He is teaching that saving faith works. Works do not earn salvation; they show it. A heart truly changed by grace will be a generous heart. And he defines true religion this way: “to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from the world” (James 1:27).

In the New Testament, care for the poor is a mark of the church. Paul’s collection for the poor in Jerusalem was a concrete act of economic solidarity between Gentile and Jewish believers.

Justice and righteousness

Two Hebrew words often appear together in the prophets: mishpat, justice, fair treatment and equal protection, and tsedaqah, righteousness, which includes active generosity. Keller argues in Generous Justice that the two are like two sides of one coin. A community that practises neither has not understood the character of God. And if you have been justified freely by grace, you will become a just person. Justice for the poor is not a political add-on to the gospel. It is its fruit.

Every poor person bears the image of God, and to ignore them is to dishonour their Maker. That is the deepest ground for caring.

Faith in action

William Wilberforce spent some twenty years in Parliament fighting the slave trade, an injustice so woven into British wealth that many thought it untouchable. He was sustained by his evangelical faith, his friendship with John Newton, and his conviction that the gospel demanded justice for the enslaved.

George Müller cared for thousands of orphans in Bristol, never asking anyone for money, trusting God to provide. For sixty years, he did.

Today, a congregation starts a food bank, a job club and a debt advice service in a poor neighbourhood. It is not replacing the gospel. It is embodying it.

For reflection

Who is the “Lazarus at your gate,” someone you pass regularly without crossing over? What is one concrete way you, or your church, could show generous justice this month?

5.title: Debt, Work, and Integrity: Practical Wisdom for Kingdom Stewards
5.essay:
The Bible is remarkably practical about money. It speaks not only about the theology of wealth but about debt, wages, contracts, taxes and honest business.

Covenant economics

The law of Moses had detailed provisions for lending (no interest charged to fellow Israelites, Deuteronomy 23:19–20), debt relief (Deuteronomy 15:1–3), fair wages paid promptly (Deuteronomy 24:14–15), and honest weights and measures (Leviticus 19:35–36). These were not side regulations. They expressed a covenant community whose economic relationships were shaped by the character of God.

The borrower is a slave

Proverbs is blunt: “The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is the slave of the lender” (Proverbs 22:7). Debt creates a kind of bondage. The wise avoid unnecessary debt, not out of fear, but because freedom — to give, to serve, to change direction, to respond to God’s call — is worth more than the things debt buys. Someone drowning in debt has few options. Someone with margin, financial and emotional, is available to God in ways the indebted person often is not.

Owe no one anything

Paul writes, “Owe no one anything, except to love each other” (Romans 13:8). This is not a ban on all borrowing; the Old Testament law assumes lending and borrowing. It is a call to honour our obligations. Unpaid debts dishonour the lender and the God who commands us to keep our word. “The wicked borrows but does not pay back” (Psalm 37:21).

And notice the contrast. The only debt never fully paid is the debt of love. We cannot love too much. We can borrow too much. The practical wisdom is to keep debts clear and manageable, so that they never limit our freedom to serve God and others. That may mean avoiding high-interest credit, buying what we can afford, and saving for what we want rather than borrowing for it. For those already in debt, it means honesty, a plan, and often help, which many churches and Christian charities offer.

Taxes and obligations

In the same chapter Paul writes, “Pay to all what is owed to them: taxes to whom taxes are owed, revenue to whom revenue is owed” (Romans 13:7). Paying taxes honestly is part of Christian integrity, even when we disagree with how they are spent. So is keeping contracts, honouring agreements, and paying what we owe on time.

Work as worship

“Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23). Paul first wrote this to slaves, people with no career and no market freedom. Even they were “serving the Lord Christ” (Colossians 3:24). Every task, however ordinary, is done for the Lord. The quality of our work is a form of testimony; the integrity of our dealings is a form of proclamation.

Fair wages

“The laborer deserves his wages” (1 Timothy 5:18). Fair pay is a matter of justice, not generosity. Christian employers are to pay fairly and promptly, and Christian employees are to give honest work for their wages.

Honest weights

“You shall have just balances, just weights,” God told Israel, and then gave the reason: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Leviticus 19:36). God identifies himself with the honest transaction, the fair price, the accurate description. To cheat in business is not only to wrong your neighbour. It is to act against the character of the God who redeemed you. The marketplace is not a God-free zone — including the till, the contract table and the salary negotiation.

The Heidelberg Catechism treats the commandment “You shall not steal” with remarkable breadth. It forbids not only open theft but every scheme to get a neighbour’s goods, whether by force or by a show of legitimacy: false weights and measures, deceptive selling, counterfeit money, excessive interest, and any other means God forbids. The Reformed tradition has always understood that economic life is moral life.

Just marketing?

Think of a business owner who reads Proverbs 11:1 — “A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight” — and realises she has been overstating her product to close sales. She had never called it lying; it was “just marketing.” The proverb cuts through the euphemism. She trains her sales team to describe the product honestly, even when it costs a sale. Within two years, customer loyalty has grown, and the honesty has built a reputation advertising never could. Honest business is often wise business, but that is a by-product, not the motive. The motive is that God hates false weights.

For reflection

Is debt limiting your freedom to serve God and others? Are there any “false weights” in your work or business — small dishonesties you have renamed as something else?

6.title: Eternal Perspective: Laying Up Treasure in Heaven
6.essay:
Jesus’ most concentrated teaching on money reaches its climax in a call to invest in what lasts.

Two kinds of treasure

“Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:19–21).

This is not an investment strategy. It is a vision of reality. There are two kinds of treasure, and only one lasts. The command is not “don’t have things,” but “don’t treasure things”: don’t deposit your heart in them, draw your security from them, or define yourself by them.

And notice the direction of Jesus’ logic. The heart follows the treasure. So one of the most powerful ways to change your heart is to change where you invest. Give, and your heart will follow where you have given.

Moneybags that do not grow old

Luke records a sharper version: “Sell your possessions, and give to the needy. Provide yourselves with moneybags that do not grow old, with a treasure in the heavens that does not fail” (Luke 12:33). Jesus is describing the direction of the kingdom: a community that holds possessions loosely enough to let them go for the sake of others. Not universal poverty, but universal generosity. What we give away in faith is kept by God for ever.

Truly life

Paul tells the wealthy “to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous and ready to share, thus storing up treasure for themselves as a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of that which is truly life” (1 Timothy 6:18–19).

This is not earning salvation. It is investing in the kingdom. And the outcome is breathtaking: that which is truly life. Not financial security, comfort or legacy, but God himself, known fully in the new creation.

What lasts

Money is temporary. At death, all of it stays behind. But relationships, character, people brought to Christ, justice done, the poor served, the church built up — these endure. Randy Alcorn speaks of an eternal investment portfolio: every act of faithful generosity is a deposit that compounds for ever. What we hold tightly stays here. What we give in faith goes on ahead.

John Wesley’s famous counsel was, “Gain all you can, save all you can, give all you can.” He earned a great deal from his books, lived simply, and died with little to his name. The rest had been given away. He did not consider himself poor. He considered himself invested.

New creation

The doctrine of new creation is the capstone of a Christian view of money. God will redeem the material world, not simply destroy it. Herman Bavinck taught that grace restores nature: the new creation is not the annihilation of the present order but its renewal and glorification. So what we do in faith with our money — the gospel work we fund, the justice we pursue, the poor we serve — is not lost. As Anthony Hoekema argued in The Bible and the Future, that hope does not make present generosity less urgent. It makes it far more meaningful.

John’s vision of the holy city includes this line: “By its light will the nations walk, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it” (Revelation 21:24). The wealth of the nations, purified and transformed, will be offered to the glory of God.

Presence, not prosperity

And the end of the story is not prosperity, but presence. “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away” (Revelation 21:3–4).

The wealth of the new creation is God himself. Every gift given in faith and every sacrifice made for the kingdom points here. We do not give to earn this. We give because we believe it. And when we believe it with our hearts and our wallets, we have understood what money is for: a temporary tool for eternal purposes, held loosely and given joyfully, until the day we need nothing, because we have everything in him.

A lifestyle cap

Think of a young couple who decide early in their marriage to set a ceiling on their standard of living, and to give away everything above it as their income grows. Twenty years later, as successful professionals, they are giving away most of what they earn. They say that decision, made early and held steadily, has been the single greatest factor in their spiritual health and their marriage. Their treasure is in heaven, and their hearts have followed it there.

For reflection

What do you actually invest in, protect, worry about and pursue? Where is your treasure? What is one step you could take this year to lay up treasure in heaven?
